newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed threatens to quit, Yeltsin says work on.
newsitem.headline: Lebed threatens to quit, Yeltsin says work on.

text.p: Alexander Lebed, Russia's outspoken national security chief, apparently threatened to resign on Thursday, forcing President Boris Yeltsin to play peacemaker among his squabbling entourage from his hospital room.
The Kremlin press service said in a statement the 65-year-old president met Lebed and dismissed the idea that he might quit after Yeltsin stripped him of one of his many posts.
Yeltsin told him to get on with his job and work more closely with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's government.

The Kremlin said Lebed objected to the appointment of Yuri Baturin, his predecessor as national security adviser, to the chair of a committee on senior military appointments -- a post Lebed had held since joining the Kremlin staff in June.

"The president stated that A.I. Lebed does not have enough grounds to raise the issue of leaving his post over this," it said. "The president urged A.I. Lebed to continue carrying out his duties and to make more effort to work with the government."
It was the first time Yeltsin had met Lebed since he appointed him his personal envoy to Chechnya on August 10.
Earlier Yeltsin, in a radio broadcast that asserted he was still in command as he prepares for heart surgery, made special mention of Lebed's role in ending the conflict in the region.
"My aide Alexander Ivanovich Lebed carried out my instruction and stopped the military conflict. The main thing is he succeeded in stopping the bloodshed," Yeltsin said.
The president has been largely out of sight since before his re-election on July 3, prompting speculation that senior figures around him are jostling for power behind the scenes.
Lebed, a 46-year-old retired paratroop general who says he wants to succeed Yeltsin, has had a lukewarm reception for his Chechen efforts from Chernomyrdin, another potential president.
A third possible presidential contender, Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov, took a new swipe at Lebed on Thursday, repeating his view that Lebed's Chechen peace deal was a "capitulation".
Lebed was roundly jeered as a "traitor" in parliament on Wednesday. Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov accused him of failing to end rebel hopes of secession from Russia.
A spokesman for Lebed told Ekho Moskvy radio there was no truth in a rumour that the security chief had threatened to resign following his hostile reception in parliament.
On Wednesday, Yeltsin's chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais denied Lebed's accusations that Kremlin aides were manipulating the president and mocked the general's appetite for publicity.
Chubais specifically cited Baturin's appointment as an example of how the Kremlin staff let Yeltsin hear a variety of arguments but left the president to make a final decision.
Lebed and Chernomyrdin met Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev in Moscow on Thursday afternoon.
Yeltsin, the press service said, told Lebed: "We must conduct the negotiations with Yandarbiyev subtly and wisely."
In his radio address, Yeltsin warned that Lebed's peace deal left problems needing further negotiations with the rebels.
"It is too soon to stop worrying," Yeltsin said. "The separatists are approaching negotiations very reluctantly."
